pairs.source_text: ubi pulsum Caecinam pergere Cremonam accepit, aegre coercitam legionem et pugnandi ardore usque ad seditionem progressam Bedriaci sistit. inter Veronam Cremonamque situs est vicus, duabus iam Romanis cladibus notus infaustusque.
pairs.question: Inter quas urbes situs est vicus Bedriacum, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: Between which cities is the village of Bedriacum situated, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Bedriacum + its location; single place fact, supported verbatim by 'inter Veronam Cremonamque situs est vicus' (the vicus is Bedriacum, named just before in 'Bedriaci sistit'). 'inter' + accusative. Tacitus's 'duabus iam Romanis cladibus' notes the two battles of Bedriacum in AD 69. Closed-book: Bedriacum, site of the AD 69 battles between Verona and Cremona, is a stock fact.

pairs.source_text: Et media acie perrupta fugere passim Othoniani, Bedriacum petentes.
pairs.question: Utrius partis copiae priore Bedriacensi proelio fusae sunt, Othonis an Vitellii, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: Whose forces were routed in the first battle of Bedriacum, Otho's or Vitellius's, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to the first battle of Bedriacum + the two contending sides; single verifiable answer, supported verbatim by 'media acie perrupta fugere passim Othoniani' (Otho's men routed, the Vitellians victorious). A/B framing keeps it decontextualizable. Closed-book: the defeat of Otho's army at the first Bedriacum is the decisive event of his short reign.

pairs.source_text: vesperascente die sitim haustu gelidae aquae sedavit. tum adlatis pugionibus duobus, cum utrumque pertemptasset, alterum capiti subdidit. et explorato iam profectos amicos, noctem quietam, utque adfirmatur, non insomnem egit: luce prima in ferrum pectore incubuit.
pairs.question: Quo modo Otho post cladem Bedriacensem sibi mortem conscivit, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: In what manner did Otho take his own life after the defeat at Bedriacum, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Otho + his death after Bedriacum; single verifiable answer, supported verbatim by 'luce prima in ferrum pectore incubuit'. Answer kept as the source's idiom 'in ferrum incubuit'. Closed-book: Otho's dignified suicide after the defeat is one of the most famous deaths in Roman history.

pairs.source_text: Othoni sepulchrum extructum est modicum et mansurum. hunc vitae finem habuit septimo et tricensimo aetatis anno.
pairs.question: Quoto aetatis anno Otho vitae finem habuit, ut Tacitus refert?
pairs.question_en: In what year of his life did Otho meet his end, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Otho's death; single number, supported verbatim by 'hunc vitae finem habuit septimo et tricensimo aetatis anno'. 'quoto aetatis anno' mirrors the ordinal idiom; answer kept as the ordinal 'septimo et tricensimo'. Closed-book number fact about Otho (died in his 37th year, AD 69).

pairs.source_text: Initium ferendi ad Vespasianum imperii Alexandriae coeptum, festinante Tiberio Alexandro, qui kalendis Iuliis sacramento eius legiones adegit. isque primus principatus dies in posterum celebratus.
pairs.question: Quis primus legiones in verba Vespasiani adegit, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: Who was the first to swear the legions into allegiance to Vespasian, per Tacitus?
pairs.answer_en: Tiberius Alexander, the prefect of Egypt.
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Vespasian's proclamation + the man who initiated it; single named person, supported verbatim by 'festinante Tiberio Alexandro, qui ... sacramento eius legiones adegit'. His office, 'praefectus Aegypti ... Alexander', is fixed at 2.74. Closed-book: the prefect of Egypt's leading the swearing-in is the famous opening of the Flavian rising.

pairs.source_text: Initium ferendi ad Vespasianum imperii Alexandriae coeptum, festinante Tiberio Alexandro, qui kalendis Iuliis sacramento eius legiones adegit. isque primus principatus dies in posterum celebratus.
pairs.question: Quibus Kalendis Tiberius Alexander legiones sacramento Vespasiani adegit, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: On which Kalends did Tiberius Alexander swear the legions to Vespasian, per Tacitus?
pairs.answer_en: On the Kalends of July (1 July).
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Tiberius Alexander + the dated oath to Vespasian; single date, supported verbatim by 'kalendis Iuliis sacramento eius legiones adegit', with 'isque primus principatus dies in posterum celebratus' confirming this became the official first day of his reign. Closed-book: the dating of Vespasian's accession to 1 July AD 69 is a stock dated fact.

pairs.source_text: Initium ferendi ad Vespasianum imperii Alexandriae coeptum, festinante Tiberio Alexandro, qui kalendis Iuliis sacramento eius legiones adegit.
pairs.question: In qua urbe initium ferendi ad Vespasianum imperii coeptum est, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: In which city did the bestowal of imperial power on Vespasian begin, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Vespasian + the start of his elevation to power; single place, supported verbatim by 'Initium ferendi ad Vespasianum imperii Alexandriae coeptum'. Locative 'Alexandriae'. Closed-book: that the Flavian principate began at Alexandria (under the prefect of Egypt) is a stock fact.

pairs.source_text: sed in tanta mole belli plerumque cunctatio; et Vespasianus modo in spem erectus, aliquando adversa reputabat: quis ille dies foret quo sexaginta aetatis annos et duos filios iuvenes bello permitteret?
pairs.question: Quot annos natus Vespasianus, cum bellum pro imperio susciperet, fuit, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: How many years old was Vespasian when he undertook the war for the throne, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Vespasian + his age at the Flavian rising; single number, supported verbatim by 'sexaginta aetatis annos ... bello permitteret' (he weighed committing his 60 years to war). 'quot annos natus' is the standard age idiom; answer kept as the number 'sexaginta'. Closed-book: Vespasian's age (about 60 in AD 69) is a stock biographical fact.

pairs.source_text: Forte inter Padum viamque patenti campo duae legiones congressae sunt, pro Vitellio unaetvicensima, cui cognomen Rapaci, vetere gloria insignis, e parte Othonis prima Adiutrix, non ante in aciem deducta, sed ferox et novi decoris avida.
pairs.question: Quae legio, in Bedriacensi proelio cum prima Adiutrice congressa, cognomen Rapacis ferebat, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: Which legion, which engaged the First Adiutrix at Bedriacum, bore the cognomen Rapax, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to the legion + its cognomen + its opponent at Bedriacum; single named legion, supported verbatim by 'pro Vitellio unaetvicensima, cui cognomen Rapaci ... e parte Othonis prima Adiutrix'. Direct question, indicative ferebat. Closed-book: Legio XXI Rapax is a well-known named legion.

pairs.source_text: Titum instare Iudaeae, Vespasianum obtinere claustra Aegypti placuit: sufficere videbantur adversus Vitellium pars copiarum et dux Mucianus et Vespasiani nomen ac nihil arduum fatis.
pairs.question: Quem ducem Vespasianus cum parte copiarum adversus Vitellium misit, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: Whom did Vespasian send as commander, with part of his forces, against Vitellius, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Vespasian + Vitellius + the Flavian commander; single named person, supported verbatim by 'sufficere videbantur adversus Vitellium pars copiarum et dux Mucianus'. Closed-book: Mucianus's leading the Flavian march on Italy (while Vespasian held Egypt and Titus pressed Judaea) is a stock fact of AD 69.

pairs.source_text: sic Capitolium ingressus atque ibi matrem complexus Augustae nomine honoravit.
pairs.question: Quo nomine Vitellius matrem suam, Capitolium ingressus, honoravit, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: With what title did Vitellius honor his mother upon entering the Capitol, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Vitellius + his mother (Sextilia, 2.64) + the title; single named honor, supported verbatim by 'matrem complexus Augustae nomine honoravit' (subject Vitellius from the sentence's start). Closed-book: Vitellius's bestowal of the title Augusta on his mother on entering Rome is a stock fact of his accession.

pairs.source_text: est Iudaeam inter Syriamque Carmelus: ita vocant montem deumque. nec simulacrum deo aut templum—sic tradidere maiores—: ara tantum et reverentia. illic sacrificanti Vespasiano, cum spes occultas versaret animo, Basilides sacerdos inspectis identidem extis...
pairs.question: In quo monte, inter Iudaeam et Syriam sito, Vespasianus sacrificavit, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: On which mountain, situated between Judaea and Syria, did Vespasian sacrifice, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Vespasian + the mountain between Judaea and Syria; single named place, supported verbatim by 'est Iudaeam inter Syriamque Carmelus: ita vocant montem deumque' and 'illic sacrificanti Vespasiano'. Closed-book: Vespasian's sacrifice on Mount Carmel and the priest Basilides's prophecy is a famous omen of his rise.

pairs.source_text: fuere quattuor legiones, e quibus bina milia praemissa; ipsae modicis intervallis sequebantur, septima a Galba conscripta, veteranae undecima ac tertia decima et praecipui fama quartadecumani, rebellione Britanniae compressa.
pairs.question: Quae legio in exercitu Othonis fama praecipua erat, ut quae rebellionem Britanniae compressisset, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: Which legion was foremost in renown in Otho's army, as having crushed the rebellion in Britain, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Otho's army + the legion that put down the British revolt; single named legion, supported verbatim by 'praecipui fama quartadecumani, rebellione Britanniae compressa'. Closed-book: Legio XIV, which crushed Boudicca's rebellion, is a well-known named legion.

pairs.source_text: Caecina Padum transgressus, temptata Othonianorum fide per conloquium et promissa, isdem petitus, postquam pax et concordia speciosis et inritis nominibus iactata sunt, consilia curasque in obpugnationem Placentiae magno terrore vertit, gnarus ut initia belli provenissent famam in cetera fore.
pairs.question: Quam coloniam, a Spurinna defensam, Caecina frustra obpugnavit, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: Which colony, defended by Spurinna, did Caecina besiege in vain, per Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Caecina (one of Vitellius's invading generals) + Spurinna + the besieged town; single named place, supported verbatim by 'consilia curasque in obpugnationem Placentiae ... vertit'. Spurinna's defense ('defensam Placentiam', 2.23) and Caecina's repulse ('multo suorum cruore pulsus Caecina', 2.21) confirm 'frustra'. Closed-book: Caecina's failed siege of Placentia is a stock episode of the Vitellian invasion of Italy.
